provenance_ruling.page_as_source: The source of record for a MISB standard is its NSG Registry document page - https://nsgreg.nga.mil/doc/view?i=<n> - and not the URL the bytes arrived over. The page is stable, dereferenceable and states the registry's own view of the document's identity: its version, its registration status and what it supersedes.
provenance_ruling.hash_as_copy: The SHA-256 identifies the COPY THAT WAS READ, which is a different claim from the edition number. This is house style in every pin record here and this round is the first to prove why it is not pedantry: ST 0601.19's cover says 02 March 2023 and the copy on disk carries two amendment rows dated after that, under the same edition number and with no minor-version letter on the cover. The edition number cannot distinguish those two documents. The hash can.
provenance_ruling.why_download_urls_are_not_recorded: The registry serves documents over EPHEMERAL PRESIGNED LINKS. Such a URL expires, so recording one would put a dead string in the source field of a record whose whole purpose is to be checkable years later. The doc/view page is what a reader is sent to; the presigned link is a transport detail of one retrieval.
provenance_ruling.what_the_edition_date_field_means: The date the DOCUMENT states for itself, read off its own cover or front matter, and authoritative for this field where the document states one. Where the registry page states a date too, both are recorded and required to agree - see st_0102_12 below, where three independent statements of 22 June 2017 agree.
provenance_ruling.the_registry_pages_were_not_machine_veri: HONEST LIMIT ON THE SOURCE FIELD. Both doc/view URLs are recorded as the citable source and neither was retrieved by this round: nsgreg.nga.mil answers an automated GET with a CAPTCHA interstitial, so the page's stated version, registration status and supersession line could not be read mechanically. They are recorded as reported. Every fact this round ASSERTS about either document - hash, byte count, page count, edition date, title-page identity - was taken from the bytes on disk instead, which is the stronger source for those five and the reason the ruling below does not rest on the registry at all. The parks' reopen route is unaffected: a CAPTCHA is a bot gate, not an account gate, and a person with a browser is not blocked.

st_0601_14.what_the_document_itself_says_about_the_: READ FROM THE PDF's OWN COVER AND REVISION HISTORY rather than inferred from the filename. (1) The cover prints 'MISB ST 0601.14a' - the letter is on the document, not only on the file. (2) Section 2 states the convention: 'In the event of a MISB document correction, the corrected document will have a single letter Minor Version appended to the Major Version number per the MISB Document Development Process [1]. For example, corrections to ST 0001.2, which has a Major Version of 2, result in a new version titled ST 0001.2a, which includes a Minor Version of "a". The MISB will not update the referring document (this document) with the Minor Version number change. When acquiring any MISB reference listed below from an NGA repository the latest version may be either a Major or Minor Version.' So the profile's failure to cite the 'a' is not an error in the profile - it is the convention working as written. (3) The revision history table on PDF page 3 says what the 'a' CHANGED, in one line: 'ST 0601.14a | 05/1/2020 | Corrected table headers in Item 47 - Generic Flags.' One corrected table header, in one item, in a 218-page document.

IT IS THE DATE OF THE 'a' MINOR REVISION AND NOT OF EDITION .14, and the next field is why that is a distinction and not a contradiction.
st_0601_14.the_two_dates_are_two_different_facts_an: NOT A CONTRADICTION, and it was checked as one before it was recorded as a distinction. Those date different things, and THE DOCUMENT ITSELF SAYS SO: its revision history table opens with the row 'ST 0601.14 | 11/1/2018' - 1 November 2018, in the MM/D/YYYY form this publisher uses throughout - and then adds 'ST 0601.14a | 05/1/2020'. Had the document's own revision history NOT carried the 11/1/2018 row, this round would have stopped and reported a contradiction between the fetched document and the registry facts it was briefed with; it carries it, so this is a distinction.

grounds: THE REPOSITORY HAS ALREADY RULED THIS, and consistency is not optional. This record's parks.shared_exit_condition, written in an earlier round and covering parks 1-7 and 9-12, reads: 'obtain the EXACT version the delegation table pins (not "the current one" - the profile pins a revision and a later revision is a different document)'. FORMAT_COVERAGE.md's park 1 row already states the hazard in its own words: 'Version .14 specifically: ST 0601 has revisions on both sides of it, and a tag added in a later revision decoded against an earlier one is a plausible number in the wrong field.' That is not a new argument produced to justify a stop; it is the argument the park was opened with.

OPTION (a) IS NOT COMPLETABLE FROM THE COPY IN HAND, which is the decisive practical ground. Option (a) requires recording 'whether any [tags] were added or changed meaning after the cited edition'. ST 0601.19's Table 1 has columns Tag, Name, Units, Format, Len, SDCC, MUL and Description - there is NO column stating which revision introduced an item - and its revision history table carries rows for .19 and its two later amendments and NO rows for .15, .16, .17 or .18. So for any given tag, 'did this exist in .14' cannot be answered from 0601.19 alone. Ruling (a) would mean asserting a delta this round cannot compute.

AND THE HAZARD IS DEMONSTRATED, not hypothetical. 0601.19's revision history records 'Resolved item 42 ambiguity (i.e., MSL or HAE)' on 06/11/2025 - a change to what a tag MEANS, on the mean-sea-level-versus-height-above-ellipsoid axis, which is exactly the class of change that yields a plausible number in the wrong field. No requirement names .16 or .18. Appendix A additionally lists retired requirements with the version each came from, including five at ST 0601.14. This bounds the REQUIREMENT delta; it does not bound the ITEM delta, and the item delta is the one a tag table would need.

tag_table_st_0601_14.how_it_was_transcribed: BY THE TABLE'S OWN DRAWN GRID, not by reading lines off a text dump, and the difference is not cosmetic. Table 1's Description cells wrap to two and three lines and are vertically CENTRED in their row, so a description line frequently sits above the line carrying its own Tag number and below the previous row's. A reader-order text extraction therefore attaches the tail of item 1's description to item 2 - which it did, on the first attempt, silently and plausibly. The transcription instead reads the page's vector rectangles: the column boundaries are the table's own vertical rules, at x = 75.4, 98.4, 217.3, 243.2, 274.2, 292.2, 317.4, 339.0 and 536.4 on every one of the five pages, and the row boundaries are the horizontal cell borders drawn in the Tag column. Each text item is then assigned to the cell its own (x, y) falls in. A cell is what the document draws, so that is what is read.
tag_table_st_0601_14.cross_check_that_makes_the_transcription: THE DOCUMENT STATES THE SAME MAPPING TWICE AND BOTH WERE READ. Table 2, 'Tags Sorted by Name' (PDF pages 17-18), is the same 141 items in alphabetical order across three name/tag column pairs - a completely different grid, extracted by the same method and independently. The two agree on all 141 tag-to-name pairs: no tag in one and not the other, and no name disagreement. Additionally the tag numbers run 1 through 141 with no gap and no duplicate, which is the positive control a summary table can offer about itself.
tag_table_st_0601_14.columns_as_the_document_defines_them: Tag, Name, Units, Format, Len, SDCC, MUL, Description - and the document defines four of them in prose immediately above the table. Units: 'None' means the value is not a measurement, 'Set' or 'Pack' means the value is a collection, 'All other Units are SI enumerations'. Format: 'the item's KLV format for the Value'. Length: 'the nominal length of the value. This may be a required length or variable length' - which is what 'V' means in the length column here. SDCC: whether the item may appear in a Standard Deviation Correlation Coefficient Floating Length Pack, whose own layout is MISB ST 1010.3's. MUL: whether the item may have multiple instances in one Local Set instance.
tag_table_st_0601_14.the_one_note_the_document_attaches_to_th: Quoted because it is a trap and the document says so itself: 'Several Local Set items have the same UL Key but differ in its Type. For example, Tag 22-Target Width, uses a Type of uint16, and Tag 96-Target Width Extended, uses a Type of IMAPB. The Key for both, which is the same, has a MISB ST 0807 dictionary data type of "float". This is an allowed practice, where this document specifies (or overrides) the metadata item's format within the dictionary.' So a decoder keyed on the 16-byte Universal Label alone cannot tell tag 22 from tag 96, and the LOCAL SET TAG is the discriminator. Recorded here rather than in a row, because it is a property of the table.

what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.why_this_node_exists: A CORRECTION TO THE REACH OF TWO EARLIER FINDINGS, and it was found by reading item 2's own section rather than by being looked for. Settlement 3 and register entry KLV 6 are both about what MISP-2019.1 does NOT state, and both are still exactly true about MISP-2019.1. What this round can now add is that the delegated dictionary states it, and the whole discipline of this section is the difference between 'the pinned documents do not say' and 'nobody has read the document that says'.
what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.the_epoch_IS_stated_here_and_it_is_state: SS 6.4, verbatim: 'Every UAS Datalink LS packet is required to include a Precision Time Stamp representing absolute time as defined in MISB ST 0603 [4]. The Precision Time Stamp (Tag 2) is an eight-byte unsigned integer counter of the number of SI Seconds (in microseconds) which have elapsed since midnight (00:00:00), January 1, 1970 (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z). Note: this time does not include leap seconds and therefore the Precision Time Stamp does not represent UTC.' SS 8.2 states it again in its own bullet and again in its Details paragraph. So epoch, unit, resolution and leap-second treatment are all read from a pinned document.
what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.what_this_corrects_in_settlement_3: NOT THE FINDING - THE REACH. Settlement 3's evidence stands unaltered: `epoch`, `1970`, `microsecond` and `leap` occur zero times in MISP-2019.1's 73 pages, and the premise that the PROFILE fixes the epoch was and is false. What changes is the consequence drawn from it. The old consequence was that this repository could not state the epoch at all without writing down something it had not read. It has now read it, in the document the profile delegates to, and the value is stated with both loci. The rule was never 'do not write an epoch'; it was 'do not write one from memory', and that rule is what allows this.
what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.what_this_corrects_in_KLV_6: KLV 6 says nothing in the profile requires a standalone metadata stream to carry an absolute time, resting on the circularity of a requirement that is 'mandatory for Metadata packets which include a Metadata item for a timestamp'. Still true of the profile. ST 0601.14 closes it from the other side for THIS local set and only for this one: SS 6.4 requires the Precision Time Stamp in every UAS Datalink LS packet, Table 1 and SS 8.2 mark item 2 Mandatory, and item 65 is Mandatory with it. A conformant UAS Datalink LS packet therefore always carries an absolute time. That is a fact about ST 0601.14's local set, not about KLV streams in general, and KLV 6 stays in the register because the general claim is the one it makes.
what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.what_it_does_NOT_settle_and_why_park_3_s: Three things. FIRST, ST 0603.5 remains the normative definition - SS 6.4 says the Precision Time Stamp represents absolute time 'as defined in MISB ST 0603 [4]' and ST 0601.14 is restating it, so a conflict between the two is resolved by a document not held. SECOND, items 136 (Leap Seconds) and 137 (Correction Offset) exist precisely to convert this scale to UTC and their own semantics are ST 0603's - and .19 later rewrote item 136's summary line to name a 'MISP Epoch', a term ST 0601.14 does not use. THIRD, what to CALL a count of SI seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z that excludes leap seconds is exactly the TAI-versus-UTC question park 3's row says it decides, and ST 0601.14 answers only the negative half: not UTC. So the row for item 2 can now state its epoch, and park 3 stays open.
what_ST_0601_14_settles_that_the_profile.the_reference_agrees_with_the_profile_wh: ST 0601.14's own reference [4] reads 'MISB ST 0603.5 MISP Time System and Timestamps, Oct 2017' - the same revision MISP-2019.1's Appendix B pins for park 3, and the same date. Two independently-pinned documents naming the same revision of a third is the corroboration delegation_table.entries was built to make checkable, and this is the first time it has been available from both sides.

framing_ruling_st_0601_14.what_this_is: THE FRAMING RULING, 2026-08-26. Parks 4 and 8 own how a key, a tag and a length are written, and this round asked the pinned copy of ST 0601.14 whether it states those rules itself. It states two of the three and delegates the third, so this node records each rule as ESTABLISHED with its section, or as UNDERIVABLE with the sentence that delegates it - and parks 4 and 8 both STAY OPEN. Nothing here flips a tag_table_st_0601_14 row: all 141 remain 'not yet', because a framing layer says where an item begins and never what it means.
framing_ruling_st_0601_14.the_document_rule_this_round_worked_unde: Where ST 0601.14a's own text and worked examples state a rule completely enough to implement and test against, the rule is recorded as established from the pinned copy with its sections cited. Where a rule exists only by reference to SMPTE ST 336 or MISB ST 0107, it is NOT reconstructed from memory or from third-party sources: it is named as underivable and the park's closure stops there. Partial closure was a permitted outcome and partial closure is what happened - and 'partial' here means the tag half of the framing, not a fraction of a park.
framing_ruling_st_0601_14.how_the_verbatim_quotations_were_obtaine: Every quotation below was read positionally from the PDF's own text runs, line by line, and not from a reader-order dump. These PDFs store text with per-glyph kerning splits, so a naive extraction renders 'BER-OID' as 'BER - OID' and '16-Byte' as '16 - Byte'; the quotations here are the glyph runs joined in x-order within each line's own y, which reproduces the printed line exactly. The same method the tag table transcription used, and the reason it is stated again is that a quotation whose whitespace was repaired by judgement is a quotation with a judgement in it.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: The packet checksum: a running 16-bit summation, its range, its algorithm, and what a receiver does when it fails.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.locus: SS 6.6, 'Packet Checksum and Version Number', PDF pages 11-12; the algorithm again at SS 8.1.1.1 and a worked vector at SS 8.1.1.2, PDF page 31.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: To help prevent erroneous metadata from being presented with the Motion Imagery, a 16-bit checksum is included in every UAS Datalink LS packet as the last item. The checksum is a running 16-bit summation through the entire packet beginning with the 16-byte Local Set Key and ending with the length field of the checksum LS item (see Figure 7).
established_from_the_pinned_copy.algorithm_verbatim: unsigned short bcc_16 ( unsigned char * buff, //Pointer to the first byte in the 16-byte UAS Datalink LS key. unsigned short len ) //Length from 16-byte US key up to 1-byte checksum length. { unsigned short bcc = 0, i; // Initialize Checksum and counter variables. for ( i = 0 ; i < len; i++) bcc += buff[i] << (8 * ((i + 1) % 2)); return bcc; } // end of bcc_16 ()
established_from_the_pinned_copy.worked_vector_verbatim: 64 bits to checksum: 060E 2B34 0200 81BB / 060E + 2B34 = 3142 / + 0200 = 3342 / + 81BB = B4FD <-- Final Checksum
established_from_the_pinned_copy.requirements_verbatim: ST 0601.8-08 All instances of a UAS Datalink LS where the computed checksum is not identical to the included checksum shall be discarded. ST 0601.8-11 All instances of the UAS Datalink LS shall contain as the final item Tag 1, (Checksum).
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: klv_codec.bcc_16, transcribed loop for loop, masked to 16 bits because Python integers do not wrap where an unsigned short does. Checked against the document's own vector rather than against itself: the eight octets 060E2B34020081BB give 0xB4FD.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.the_half_that_is_still_blocked: SS 6.6 defines the checksum's RANGE in terms of 'the length field of the checksum LS item', so finding that end means walking the local set, which means the length grammar. bcc_16 therefore takes the range as an argument exactly as the standard's own C does, and this repository offers nothing that computes it. The algorithm is established; applying it to a real packet is not.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: A Zero-Length Item is a tag followed by a length of zero and no value, and it means the value is now unknown.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: If a metadata producer needs to “shut-off” an item (i.e. make it immediately Unknown) the producer sends a Zero-Length Item (ZLI) which is a Local Set item with no value (i.e. tag followed by a length of zero, with no value).

Recorded here so that the walk, when it is written, is written knowing it. Not implementable now for the same reason nothing else is: a length of zero still has to be read as a length.

CAT034 Phase 1 found the first file where they disagree and recorded the divergence; the harmonisation round ruled for the page tree and rewrote this field. ambiguity_register.KLV 1: The promulgation lag. The wrapper's cover, Letter of Promulgation and reference are all dated 30 July 2020; the profile it promulgates carries November 2018 on its title page and in the footer of all 73 pages. Twenty months, unexplained in either document. Sharpened by the profile's own FORWARD versioning rule, which makes the '2019' in MISP-2019.1 an identifier rather than a date - so citing this content by year is ambiguous between 2018 printed, 2019 in the identifier and 2020 promulgated. Consequence adopted: every citation names the document by identifier and hash, never by date.
ambiguity_register.KLV 2: Every requirement ID inside MISP-2019.1 names an earlier profile version. 120 distinct requirement IDs occur and NONE is MISP-2019.1-nn. Distribution: MISP-2015.1 93, MISP-2018.1 17, MISP-2016.1 8, MISP-2018.3 4, MISP-2018.2 3, MISP-2017.1 3, MISP-2015.3 1. The prefix records the profile version that INTRODUCED the requirement, not the document carrying it, so MISP-2015.1-07 is a live requirement of MISP-2019.1. Consequence adopted: requirements are cited by their own ID with the pinned document named beside them, because an ID alone reads to a NATO reader as a citation of MISP-2015.1 - which STANAG 4609 Edition 4 promulgated and Edition 5 superseded.
ambiguity_register.KLV 3: The profile's reference to the STANAG is one edition behind and its Appendix C is one edition ahead. Appendix B ref [1] is 'NATO STANAG 4609: NATO Digital Motion Imagery Standard, Edition 4, 19 Dec 2016' and SS 1.1 sends the reader to [1] for NATO-specific requirements; Appendix C.1.2 discusses 'STANAG 4609 Edition 5 as represented in MISP-2019.1'. So within one document the STANAG is both Edition 4 and Edition 5, and the wrapper actually holding this profile is Edition 5, which supersedes Edition 4. A reader following SS 1.1's pointer lands on the superseded edition.
ambiguity_register.KLV 4: External context, and explicitly not an error: the NISP is a year behind the chain. NISP Volume 1, ADatP-34(L) / Version 12, 19 Jul 2019, 182 pages, lists NATO STANAG 4609 as 'Ed 4' against 'Standard - MISP-2015.1'. That NISP version predates STANAG 4609 Edition 5 by a year, so it is stale by chronology rather than by mistake - which means a programme taking the NISP as its authority would implement MISP-2015.1 and be conformant to a superseded STANAG. The copy read hashes to 12a3b2ab7075390b9edd53fb50538f5a7098c0d8f0a9a69c8af894acb40e1bac, 1440024 bytes, and is NOT in fixtures/klv/spec/ - so that hash stands on the reading that recorded it and is the one value here a later re-verification cannot check. Same treatment AEDP-12 Edition A (2014) gets in the NITS pin: history, never a basis.
ambiguity_register.KLV 5: The reference list versions most of its MISB documents and six not at all. A revision suffix is given for every document this row set relies on (0601.14, 0102.12, 0603.5, 0107.3, 0903.4, 0806.4, 1402.2, 1201.3, 1303.1, 1204.1, 0902.8) and none for ref [74] 'MISB ST 1607 Constructs to Amend/Segment KLV Metadata, 2016', ref [89] 'MISB ST 1101', ref [84] 'MISB RP 1302' or the three TRMs at refs [98], [99], [100]. ST 1607 is the one that bites: MISP-2017.1-95 is a 'shall' whose target names no revision.
ambiguity_register.KLV 6: Nothing in the profile requires a standalone metadata stream to carry an absolute time. The unconditional mandate MISP-2018.3-116 attaches to a Motion Imagery FRAME; the metadata mandate MISP-2018.1-97 is conditional on a timestamp being present; the prose in SS 2.1.5 introducing both is circular - 'it is also mandatory for Metadata packets which include a Metadata item for a timestamp based on Absolute Time'. The two unequivocal predecessors MISP-2015.1-03 and MISP-2015.1-04 are in Appendix A.2 as DEPRECATED. SS 5.5 then contemplates the case that falls through: 'There are situations where Metadata needs to be transmitted separately from the Motion Imagery.' ambiguity_register.KLV 7: The security mandate's paragraph and its requirement do not use the same term, and Appendix E defines both. SS 4.4.2.9 says 'It is mandatory that Motion Imagery Data be marked correctly and consistently with security classification' and 'The approved practices in this standard are mandatory for all Motion Imagery Data'; the requirement it introduces, MISP-2015.1-73, says 'Motion Imagery shall include Security Metadata'. Appendix E defines 'Motion Imagery Data' as 'Three components: Motion Imagery (see definition below), Metadata and/or Audio' and 'Motion Imagery' as a sequence of pictures. So the paragraph's scope includes a metadata stream and the requirement's scope is the imagery, which decides whether this adapter's input must be labelled at all.
ambiguity_register.KLV 8: The document classified as 'related' is the one that 'defines the required data items'. STANAG 4609 Ed 5 puts the Motion Imagery Handbook under OTHER RELATED DOCUMENTS while its AGREEMENT clause names only MISP-2019.1, and MISP SS 1.3 calls the Handbook a companion 'providing definitions of terms used with more background and technical detail'. But SS 3.6.7 says of the same document that it 'defines the Structure of the Common Metadata System (CMS), describes how to organize the sensor/platform data into a hierarchy of KLV Packs and Local Sets that reduces the bandwidth needed to transmit the data, and defines the required data items'. A document that defines required data items is normative in fact. Park 10 records that whoever obtains it answers this first.
ambiguity_register.KLV 9: A pinned copy whose cover does not describe its contents, and the first ambiguity in this record found by a check nobody asked for. ST 0601.19's cover reads 'MISB ST 0601.19' and '02 March 2023'; its revision history table carries two rows dated AFTER that cover date - 05/10/2024, changing Figure 17's corner 4 tag values, and 06/11/2025, resolving 'item 42 ambiguity (i.e., MSL or HAE)' - and the file's /CreationDate is 2 July 2025. The document's own section 2 states the convention it is not following: a corrected document 'will have a single letter Minor Version appended to the Major Version number', as ST 0001.2 becomes ST 0001.2a, and the MISB 'will not update the referring document with the Minor Version number change'. So there exist at least three distinct documents all correctly cited as 'ST 0601.19', a citation by edition number cannot distinguish them, and the same section warns that 'when acquiring any MISB reference listed below from an NGA repository the latest version may be either a Major or Minor Version'. WHAT IT BOUNDS: it does not affect this round's ruling, which stops on .14-versus-.19 and would stop identically whichever .19 copy were held. What it bounds is the claim a pin makes - which is why this record's SHA-256 is the identity of a COPY and not of an edition, and this is the first document in this repository where those two come apart. ST 0102.12 was checked the same way and does not have the problem: one revision-history row, and it is the cover date.
ambiguity_register.KLV 10: THE SAME COMING-APART AS KLV 9, MET AT FETCH TIME INSTEAD OF BEING DISCOVERED LATER, and one turn worse in each of two ways. MISP-2019.1 cites 'MISB ST 0601.14'; the NSG Registry serves that edition as ST0601.14a.pdf; the file's cover reads 'MISB ST 0601.14a' and '1 May 2020' while the edition the citation names is dated 1 November 2018 by the document's own revision history. ST 0601.19's two undeclared amendments at least sat under a stable edition number that a citation could name; this one has no string at all, so there is no citation any document could make that would distinguish it. Item 65, UAS Datalink LS Version Number, is MANDATORY in every packet and states the revision of ST 0601 the producer encoded against - and it is a uint8, one value per MAJOR revision, so it cannot express a Minor Version letter either. The format's own answer to 'which edition made this?' has exactly the same blind spot as the citation. ambiguity_register.KLV 11: THREE DELEGATED DOCUMENTS THIS REPOSITORY HOLDS PIN ST 336:2017 AND ONE PINS ST 336:2007, and it was found by reading reference lists this round had no other reason to read. MISP-2019.1's Appendix B ref [13] reads 'SMPTE ST 336:2017 Data Encoding Protocol Using Key-Length-Value' and ST 0601.14a's own reference [2] reads the same string - so the profile and the field dictionary agree. ST 0102.12's reference [3] reads 'SMPTE ST 336:2007 Data Encoding Protocol Using Key-Length-Value', a DIFFERENT EDITION, and it is not decorative there: ST 0102.12-65 says 'The Security Metadata Universal Set shall conform to SMPTE ST 336 KLV encoding rules' and ST 0102.12-66 says the same of the Local Set. WHY IT MATTERS AND WHY IT IS REGISTERED RATHER THAN RESOLVED: park 8 is a single row naming a single edition, and these are two. A round that buys ST 336:2017 will hold the grammar ST 0601's items are framed under and will NOT hold the one ST 0102's security items are required to conform to, and this record cannot say whether the two editions differ in any way that reaches a length octet - because neither is held. NOT A CONTRADICTION IN EITHER DOCUMENT: each is internally consistent and each pins what was current when it was written, ST 0102.12 in June 2017 and ST 0601.14 in November 2018. It is a divergence between two delegations of one profile, which is a fact about the profile's reference set rather than about either standard. WHAT IT BOUNDS: park 8's exit condition, which now has a question in it that the parks table's 'obtain the EXACT version the delegation table pins' does not answer, since the delegation table pins one edition and two of the held documents pin two. Recorded, not acted on: changing a park's exit condition on the strength of a reference list read in passing is the roster change smuggled into a reading that the park 1 round refused to make. UPDATED 2026-08-26 BY THE LENGTH ROUND, AND THE COUNT MOVED FROM TWO-AGAINST-ONE TO THREE-AGAINST-ONE: MISB ST 0107.3's reference [1] reads 'SMPTE ST 336:2017 Data Encoding Protocol Using Key-Length-Value', agreeing with ST 0601.14a's ref [2] and MISP-2019.1's Appendix B ref [13]. ambiguity_register.KLV 12: A HELD DOCUMENT'S REQUIREMENT IDENTIFIERS DO NOT ALL CARRY ITS OWN EDITION NUMBER, and citing them as though they did would cite strings the document does not contain. MISB ST 0107.3 states thirteen requirements. Eleven are prefixed ST 0107.3 (-03 through -13) and TWO are prefixed ST 0107.2: 'ST 0107.2-01 Bit order shall be big-endian or msb' and 'ST 0107.2-02 Byte order shall be big-endian or MSB', both in section 6.1. NOT AN ERROR IN THE DOCUMENT: MISB stamps a requirement with the edition that introduced it, and this edition's own revision history says it 'Added requirements -03 through -13', which confirms -01 and -02 came from ST 0107.2 - registry document 4149, which 0107.3 supersedes. So the numbering runs continuously across editions and the prefix is provenance rather than a typo. WHY IT IS REGISTERED RATHER THAN NOTED IN PASSING: klv_codec.decode_ber_length reads its long-form payload big-endian on ST 0107.2-02's authority, and it is the ONLY octet-order requirement in the whole delegation chain - ST 0601.14a never states one. A citation this load-bearing that is easy to normalise to 'ST 0107.3-02' is exactly the miscitation that gets made once and then propagates to five sites. HOW TO CHECK IT: the two requirement blocks sit under section 6.1 on PDF page 2 and print the 0107.2 prefix in the document's own left column.
ambiguity_register.KLV 13: A HELD DOCUMENT NAMES ASN.1 AS THE SOURCE OF THE BER RULES AND PINS THE PART OF ASN.1 THAT DOES NOT CONTAIN THEM. MISB ST 0107.3 SS 6.3.3.1 says, verbatim: 'Items using "ber" types in the MISB standards use the ASN.1 [4] Basic Encoding Rules for Lengths rules.' And SS 6.3.1 says of tags: 'The Basic Encoding Rules (BER) for an Object Identifier (BER-OID) as defined in ASN.1 [4] is the method selected for encoding a Local Set tag', and later 'ASN.1 forbids the use of 0x80 in the first byte of a BER-OID value'. Its reference [4] reads 'ITU Rec X.680 (08/15) Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1): Specification of basic notation'. X.680 SPECIFIES NOTATION; the Basic Encoding Rules are X.690. So the document attributes an encoding rule to the ASN.1 recommendation that defines syntax rather than encoding. WHY IT IS REGISTERED AND NOT RESOLVED: neither X.680 nor X.690 is held, so this repository cannot say whether X.680 (08/15) contains anything that bears on BER lengths, nor whether the citation is a slip or a convention of the series. IT IS NOT A CONTRADICTION IN ST 0107.3 - the document is internally consistent and says the same thing in both places. WHAT IT BOUNDS, AND THIS IS WHY IT MATTERS: park 8's reopen condition reads 'A PURCHASE DECISION, NOT A DOWNLOAD' because SMPTE paywalls ST 336. ITU recommendations are free. If the BER rules the two remaining residues need - the meaning of a zero length-of-length, and any ceiling on length octets - are in X.690 rather than in ST 336, then part of the one park that costs money is a free download. NOT ACTED ON: the reference needs adjudicating first, and changing a park's reopen route on a reference list read in passing is the roster change the park 1 round refused to make. A round that wants park 8 cheaper starts here.
ambiguity_register.KLV 14: THE FORMAT CARRIES A MANDATORY EDITION STAMP ON THE WIRE AND NO HELD EDITION SAYS WHICH ITEMS EACH EDITION ADMITS. MISB ST 0601 requires item 65 in every packet (ST 0601.8-12) and SS 8.65 defines its value as the document's own major revision, '1..255 corresponds to document revisions MISB ST 0601.1 thru MISB ST 0601.255'. So every conforming packet declares the edition it was written against, and a reader that wanted to honour that declaration would need to know WHICH ITEMS THAT EDITION DEFINES. NEITHER HELD COPY PROVIDES IT, IN EITHER DIRECTION. ST 0601.14a's revision history begins at edition 14 and ST 0601.19's at edition 19; no item section in either carries an introduction annotation; Table 1's own column list - Tag, Name, Units, Format, Len, SDCC, MUL, Description - has no edition column; and the one dating device the series does carry, the requirement-identifier prefix, is stamped only from edition 8 onward, so ST 0601.14a's 33 distinct identifiers span editions 8, 9, 10, 13 and 14 and NONE reaches editions 1 through 7. WHAT IT BOUNDS: reconciliation_ruling had already recorded, looking FORWARD from .14, that the requirement delta to .19 is enumerable from the stamps but 'does not bound the ITEM delta, and the item delta is the one a tag table would need'. The walk round looked BACKWARD from .14 to .1 and met the same wall from the other side. So the item delta is not enumerable in EITHER direction from anything held, and the stamp a conforming emitter is REQUIRED to send cannot be acted on by a reader holding these documents. NOT A CONTRADICTION - no held sentence disagrees with another - and NOT RESOLVABLE HERE: it is resolved by holding the editions themselves, which for edition 1 is PARK 13. It is the reason that park exists and the reason the walk round ended in a park rather than a ruling. || AMENDED 2026-08-27 BY THE PARKS ROUND, AND THE AMENDMENT ABOVE IS PARTLY REFUTED. The park-13 closure concluded that 'the wall is made of unobtained documents rather than of undocumented history - the editions state their own deltas perfectly well'. The second half is false, and the documents that refute it were on disk when it was written: they landed in spec/history/ at 20:42 on 2026-08-26 and the amendment was written the same day. THE CHECK, which needs no changelog at all: an edition's item SET is readable from its own SS 7 / SS 8 subsection headers, and six editions are held. Enumerated, contiguous, no gaps in any of them - EG0601 initial release 1..39 (39); EG 0601.1 1..72 (72); STD 0601.4 1..80 (80); MISB ST 0601.8 1..95 (95); ST 0601.14a 1..141 (141); ST 0601.19 1..143 (143). EDITION 1'S CHANGELOG BALANCES EXACTLY: 'Added metadata items 40 through 72', and 39 + 33 = 72, confirmed at both endpoints - which is what park 13's closure leaned on and it holds. EDITIONS 2 THROUGH 4 DO NOT. Eight items separate edition 1 from edition 4 (73-80) and ST 0601.4's SS 3 accounts for FOUR: the RVT nesting tag at .2 (73), and at .3 the VMTI nesting tag (74) plus the 'Reference Ellipsoid Height versions of Sensor and Alternate Platform heights' (75, 76). Items 77 Operational Mode, 78 Frame Center Height Above Ellipsoid, 79 Sensor North Velocity and 80 Sensor East Velocity are named in NO SS 3 row - the words 'operational' and 'velocity' occur nowhere in that section - and .4's own row adds no item. So the surviving changelog is INCOMPLETE WHERE IT EXISTS, not merely absent where it does not. WHAT IT BUYS: the item set is known exactly at six editions rather than two, editions 2 and 3 are bounded between 72 and 80 with four of eight additions attributed, and the wall is now editions 5, 6, 7 and 9 through 13 and 15 through 18 - fourteen, none held. The pricing changes with it: obtaining an edition buys its TABLE, because a table always states itself; it does not reliably buy its DELTA. A reader honouring a stamp of 0x0B still has nothing to consult, which is this entry's point and is untouched.
ambiguity_register.KLV 15: THE DOCUMENT THE STANDARD TELLS A READER TO CONSULT FOR EDITION 1 DOES NOT EXIST UNDER THAT NAME. ST 0601.14a SS 8.65 defines item 65's value as '1..255 corresponds to document revisions MISB ST 0601.1 thru MISB ST 0601.255', so a reader honouring an on-the-wire stamp of 0x01 is sent to 'MISB ST 0601.1'. NO SUCH DOCUMENT WAS EVER PUBLISHED: edition 1 of the series is MISB EG 0601.1, an ENGINEERING GUIDELINE dated 15 May 2008 on its cover, and the series became a Standard at 0601.2 - ST 0601.4 SS 3 states the conversion outright ('Change the status from Engineering Guideline to Standard in order to enforce requirements upon developers implementing this document'). The standard has renamed its own history, and SS 8.65's range projects the ST name back across twelve editions that did not carry it. EDITION 1 SAYS SO ITSELF, from the other side: its own SS 7.65 states the identical range as 'EG0601.1 thru EG0601.255'. WHAT IT COST: park 13 was opened, described, guarded by a test and cited from three files under the name 'MISB ST 0601.1', and the name was wrong in every one of them - which is not a drafting slip in this repository but SS 8.65's own naming, adopted without checking that the document existed. IT ALSO NEARLY COST THE FETCH: the Wayback CDX index holds no ST0601.1.pdf at gwg.nga.mil because that filename never existed, and the document was found at /misb/docs/eg/EG0601.1.pdf only after the search was widened past the name the park gave it. NOT A CONTRADICTION between held sentences - SS 8.65 and SS 7.65 describe the same range and the series really did change status - and RESOLVED for this repository's purposes: park 13 is closed on EG 0601.1, which is the document SS 8.65's '0601.1' denotes, and the closure says so in as many words rather than quietly correcting the name.
ambiguity_register.KLV 16: EDITION 1 DISAGREES WITH ITSELF ABOUT ITS OWN DATE, AND ST 0601.4 DISAGREES WITH IT AGAIN. EG 0601.1's cover prints '15 May 2008' and no page header or footer in its 98 pages carries a date, so the cover is its sole statement and under provenance_ruling.what_the_edition_date_field_means it governs the pin's edition_date field. Its own SS 3, however, carries TWO rows for EG0601.1 - '13 December 2007' and '15 May 2007' - which puts the row described as 'Editorial changes only' seven months BEFORE the substantive one, and puts it a year before the cover. ST 0601.4's SS 3 restates the same first row as '13 December 2006', which makes the sequence coherent (13 Dec 2006, then 15 May 2007) and disagrees with edition 1's own text by a year. So of the three readings available, the two that are internally coherent are the ones edition 1 does NOT state. NOT RESOLVED AND DELIBERATELY SO: nothing held decides which year is the typo, the pin records the cover date because the ruling says the document's own cover governs, and NO RULING IN THIS REPOSITORY RESTS ON THE DATE - park 13 turned on a Len column, not on a calendar. Recorded because the pin states one date and the document contains three, and a reader checking the pin against the PDF will meet the other two. || THE COVER DATE IS CORROBORATED FROM INSIDE THE DOCUMENT ON 2026-08-27, by a route nobody had tried: edition 1's own reference list. EG 0601.1's SS 2.3 cites 'MISB RP 0102.5, Security Metadata Universal and Local Sets for Digital motion Imagery, 15 May 2008'. WHAT THAT PROVES, EXACTLY: a document cannot cite a reference published a year after itself, so the held bytes CANNOT be the 15 May 2007 issue - the copy pinned here is the 15 May 2008 one, and any reading in which this PDF is the 2007 issue is dead. The edition_date field does not move; what moves is its standing, from a value ELECTED by provenance_ruling to a value CORROBORATED at a second site inside the same 98 pages. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE, and this entry declines to round up: WHY SS 3 reads 2007. Two readings survive and the bytes do not separate them - (a) SS 3's year is a one-digit typo and the row is the cover's own issue, or (b) there was a real 15 May 2007 editorial issue and the document was re-issued on 15 May 2008 without SS 3 gaining a row for it. (a) IS THE BETTER READING AND IS NOT A PROOF: two issues falling on the same day and month a year apart is a coincidence where a single mistyped digit is the commonest defect in this register, and SS 3 exists to log revisions - its own first row is 'Added section 3 for modifications and changes' - so a re-issue it does not log is a defect of the same size as the typo it would replace. UNDER EITHER READING ST 0601.4's SS 3 DOES NOT REPAIR THAT ROW: it restates 2007. So this entry's own sentence that .4's restatement 'makes the sequence coherent' is true of ONE of the two rows, and that is this round's correction to it. TWO FURTHER ANCHORS, both first-hand: the initial release is 12 January 2006 at two independent sites (EG 0601's cover and ST 0601.4's SS 3), and ST 0601.4's SS 3 dates STD 0601.2 to October 29, 2008. STILL UNDECIDED: both SS 3 rows, for different reasons - the '15 May' row is narrowed to two readings, and the '13 December' row is UNTOUCHED, 13 December 2007 by edition 1's SS 3 against 13 December 2006 by ST 0601.4's, with nothing held separating them at all. NO RULING IN THIS REPOSITORY RESTS ON THE DATE and that has not changed. Note the designation in the citation: RP 0102.5, not ST 0102.5. The 0102 series converted Recommended Practice to Standard exactly as the 0601 series converted Engineering Guideline to Standard, so this is KLV 15's phenomenon one series over - and it is what made the delegation-table gate refuse the edit until the revision was declared.
ambiguity_register.KLV 17: TWO EDITIONS FILL THE FORMAT COLUMN OF ITEMS 11 AND 12 DIFFERENTLY, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS A CHARACTER ENCODING. ST 0601.14a SS 8.11 and SS 8.12 both state a KLV Format of 'utf8' with a Max Length of 127. MISB EG 0601.1 SS 7.11 and SS 7.12 both state 'ISO7' with a stated range of '1..127', and edition 1's Table 1 writes the same two items as 'String ISO7'. THIS IS THE ONLY COLUMN THAT MOVED. The witnessed-set round of 2026-08-26 read all 26 witnessed items at both ends of a twelve-year span - edition 1 (15 May 2008) and .14a (1 May 2020) - and every other Units, Range and Format cell agrees. WHAT IT COSTS: nothing on any octet either edition admits, because ISO 646 is a strict subset of UTF-8 by construction, so klv_uas_codec decodes both as UTF-8 - the PINNED edition's statement, which reconciliation_ruling requires. WHAT IT WOULD COST IF IGNORED: an emitter written against edition 1 sending a high-bit octet meant as an 8-bit code page produces a value that is not valid UTF-8, and decode_value refuses it naming this entry. The pinned stream says nothing either way - its own items 11 and 12 are pure ASCII ('EON', 'IR', 'Geodetic WGS84'). NOT A CONTRADICTION BETWEEN HELD SENTENCES: the series changed its own encoding somewhere in the twelve revisions between the two, and which revision is a question no held changelog answers - the .5, .6, .7 and .9-through-.13 gap the park 13 adjudication round already named. || NARROWED FROM TWELVE REVISIONS TO FIVE ON 2026-08-27, and the intermediate step turns out not to be an encoding change at all. This entry was written from the two ENDPOINTS of the span; the lineage holds two documents INSIDE it. Items 11 and 12, Format column, verbatim, at all six held editions: EG0601 initial release 'String ISO7' (and 'String 1..127 ISO7' in the item blocks); EG 0601.1 'String 1..127 ISO7'; STD 0601.4 'String 1..127 ISO7' - UNCHANGED AT EDITION 4; MISB ST 0601.8 'String 1..127 ISO 646' - A THIRD SPELLING; ST 0601.14a 'utf8'; ST 0601.19 'utf8'. EDITION 8'S 'ISO 646' IS A RENAMING AND NOT A CHANGE, and edition 8 is the document that proves it: its reference [16] is 'ISO/IEC 646:1991, Information Technology - ISO 7-bit coded Character Set for Information Interchange' - the standard 'ISO7' had denoted for eight editions without ever citing it. So the column moved TWICE and only the second move is an encoding change: ISO7 -> ISO 646 between editions 4 and 8, naming the same character set, and ISO 646 -> utf8 between editions 8 and 14. The gap shrinks from .2-through-.13 to .9-through-.13, five revisions, none held. AND THE REFERENCE WENT WITH THE COLUMN: ST 0601.14a's reference list contains no ISO 646 entry at all - '646' occurs twice in its 218 pages and neither occurrence is a reference - so the edition that adopted utf8 dropped the normative reference for the encoding it replaced rather than superseding it in place. ONE RESIDUE, inside a single edition rather than between two: ST 0601.8 states the Format as 'ISO 646' in the item blocks and still carries the note '- ISO7 character set.' at three sites in the same document. Both spellings denote reference [16], so it is a drafting residue and not a contradiction - and it is the evidence that edition 8 is the RENAMING edition, because it is the one edition where the old spelling and the new one appear together. COSTS NOTHING on any octet any of the six editions admits, for the reason above; klv_uas_codec is unchanged.

parks.how_many: Thirteen parks over fifteen documents, and THREE are CLOSED - park 1, park 4 and park 13. Ten remain open, nine of them public downloads and one a purchase. PARK 13 CLOSED 2026-08-26 BY THE ADJUDICATION ROUND, on the same day it was opened by the walk round, and it is the only park in this table that opened and closed inside one day. It is also the only one a STREAM asked for rather than a document: it was a superseded revision of a document this repository already holds at a later edition, which under this repository's own rule - a later revision is a different document - makes it a fifteenth document and not a re-read of the third. THE FIFTEENTH DOCUMENT TURNED OUT NOT TO BE NAMED WHAT THIS TABLE CALLED IT: there is no MISB ST 0601.1, edition 1 is MISB EG 0601.1, and the park closed on that document - see ambiguity_register KLV 15 and park_13_ruling_2026_08_26. THE DELEGATION COUNT DOES NOT MOVE AND IS NOT THE SAME COUNT: the profile delegates to FOURTEEN documents, park 13's document is not one of them, and a park's document and a profile's delegation are different things. THE NUMBERING DOES NOT MOVE: the parks are cited by number from the row sets, from the fixture plan and from the register, so a closed park keeps its number and its row and says it is closed, and a new park extends the numbering rather than filling a gap. Renumbering to close a gap would silently re-point every citation, which is a larger lie than a table with three closed rows in it.
parks.honest_strength: Of the ten that remain open, nine are public downloads and one is not. That is materially weaker than the two blockers this repository already carries - GMTIF's Annex L, which reads '(TO BE PROVIDED)' in the promulgated text, and the NITS XSD, which the Custodian re-issues on its own revision axis and distributes through national representatives. It is closer to CAT048's Reserved Expansion Field: obtainable, and simply not obtained. PARKS 1, 4 AND 13 ARE THE PROOF OF THAT CLAIM RATHER THAN EXCEPTIONS TO IT - the largest park in the table, the cheapest, and the narrowest were all closed by one person with a browser, which is what 'obtainable, and simply not obtained' predicts. Park 4 is the sharpest of the three proofs: it was SIX PAGES, it had been sitting behind a free download since November 2018, and it held the rule that stopped this repository reading a KLV stream at all. PARK 13 IS THE SECOND-SHARPEST AND IT SHARPENS A DIFFERENT EDGE: its document was not behind a free download at all - both official routes refuse an automated GET - and it was obtained anyway, from a mirror of the publisher's own host, which says that 'obtainable' can survive the publisher's front door being shut and that the honest cost of that is a provenance caveat rather than a stop. See delegated_specifications_held.eg_0601_1.source_is_a_MIRROR_and_not_the_registry.

the_one_that_is_not_a_download.reopen_condition: A PURCHASE DECISION, NOT A DOWNLOAD. SMPTE is a commercial standards body and ST 336 sits behind a paywall, which the profile concedes in its own register: 'Commercial references cited in this document are available from industry organizations.' The other nine open parks need somebody to spend an afternoon; this one needs somebody to spend money, and a table reporting both as 'obtain the document' would hide the only entry that has to go to a person with a budget.
the_one_that_is_not_a_download.what_the_length_round_learned_about_this: IT SHRANK AGAIN AND IT DID NOT MOVE. MISB ST 0107.3 - a free six-page download - states the length grammar and the BER-OID chain rule, so what park 8 still owns is two ABSENCES in ST 0107.3 rather than a grammar: 0x80 as a first length octet, and any ceiling on the count of length octets. Neither is reachable from a conforming stream. AND THE COST MAY NOT BE WHAT THIS FIELD SAYS: ST 0107.3 SS 6.3.3.1 sources the BER length rules to ASN.1 [4], an ITU recommendation, and ITU recommendations are free. That is registered as KLV 13 and NOT acted on here, because its reference [4] is X.680 - notation - where BER is X.690, so the citation needs adjudicating before this field is rewritten.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: The short form: for lengths below 128, one octet, and the octet IS the length.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: For example, encoding the length of two (2), a value less than 128, with long form uses two bytes (0x8102) instead of the short form one-byte (0x02) length.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.how_it_is_derived: The document prints 0x02 as the short form of 2 and names 'values less than 128' as the range for which long form is the wasteful choice. So 0..127 is one octet with no flag bit to strip.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: The long form: the first octet's low seven bits are the COUNT of following octets, and those octets are the length big-endian.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.locus: SS 6.3.2, PDF page 4, for the form; ST 0107.2-01 and ST 0107.2-02 in SS 6.1, PDF page 2, for the octet order.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: BER is an efficient encoding of a length; however, by either using the long form for values less than 128, or by prepending a long form value with zero-byte values, BER becomes less efficient. For example, encoding the length of two (2), a value less than 128, with long form uses two bytes (0x8102) instead of the short form one-byte (0x02) length. Another example is encoding the value 128 with padded zeros (0x8300 0080) instead of the optimized value with two bytes (0x8180).
established_from_the_pinned_copy.how_it_is_derived: THE DERIVATION WRITTEN OUT, because this is the clause a recollection would have supplied. The passage prints four encodings of two lengths: 0x02 -> 2 short form; 0x81 0x02 -> 2 long form with ONE following octet; 0x81 0x80 -> 128 long form with ONE following octet; 0x83 0x00 0x00 0x80 -> 128 long form with THREE following octets. 0x81 introduces one and 0x83 introduces three, so the low seven bits of the first octet are a count. The document also states how it COUNTS: it calls 0x8180 'two bytes' and 0x8102 'two bytes', so the introducer is included in the total. The following octets are big-endian by ST 0107.2-02, 'Byte order shall be big-endian or MSB'. Two data points plus an octet-order requirement fix the shape uniquely, and nothing is imported from outside the document.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.second_statement_verbatim: ST 0107.3-05 All instances of item Length fields within a MISB defined KLV Universal or Local Set shall be BER Short form or BER Long form encoded using the fewest possible bytes.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: klv_codec.decode_ber_length and encode_ber_length. Fixtures length_long_form_lowest (8180, the document's own), length_long_form_two_octets and length_non_minimal_padded_zeros (83000080, the document's own).

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: Minimal encoding is REQUIRED. An encoder does NOT choose freely between the forms.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.locus: ST 0107.3-05, SS 6.3.2, PDF page 4. LIVE text, not deprecated.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: All instances of item Length fields within a MISB defined KLV Universal or Local Set shall be BER Short form or BER Long form encoded using the fewest possible bytes.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.this_is_the_answer_to_park_4s_question: YES to minimality, NO to free choice. And it is the same sentence ST 0601.14a carries as ST 0601.8-07 with two edits: the onward delegation 'in accordance with SMPTE ST 336 [2]' is REMOVED, and the scope widens from 'a UAS Datalink LS packet' to 'a MISB defined KLV Universal or Local Set'. ST 0601.14a's revision history said the content moved here 'as they apply to all MISB KLV based metadata (not just ST 0601)'; this is the content, and it arrived without the delegation. So the constraint is ST 0107.3's own and does not route onward to park 8.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.what_it_makes_possible: A TOTAL encoder with no form selector. For every length there is exactly one conforming encoding, so encode_ber_length takes the length and nothing else - the ruling is enforced by the signature rather than by a check. test_the_length_codec_is_total_because_st_0107_3_05_leaves_no_choice_of_form asserts the parameter list.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: klv_codec.decode_ber_length refuses both non-minimal forms as KLVFramingError; encode_ber_length cannot express either.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: The two non-minimal forms, named and refused: long form for a value below 128, and leading zero octets.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: by either using the long form for values less than 128, or by prepending a long form value with zero-byte values, BER becomes less efficient
established_from_the_pinned_copy.why_exactly_two_and_not_a_general_policy: Because the document names exactly two and works an example against each. A codec refusing 'non-minimal encodings' in general would be enforcing a rule nobody wrote; a codec refusing these two is enforcing SS 6.3.2's sentence. They happen to be exhaustive over the long form - a long-form encoding is minimal iff its value is at least 128 and its leading octet is non-zero - and that they coincide is worth stating rather than relying on.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: Two KLVFramingError branches, each quoting the document's own example against the octets in hand. Fixtures length_non_minimal_long_form (8102) and length_non_minimal_padded_zeros (83000080).

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: A zero length is legal, and the Value is then absent rather than empty.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: The Length defines the number of bytes used by the Value. Lengths are usually positive numbers; however, a zero length is possible in unique cases. Values are the binary representation describing a specific item. In the case of a zero Length, the Value is not a part of the item (see MISB ST 0601 [3]).
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: encode_ber_length(0) is 0x00 and walk_local_set advances past such an item without consuming a value octet. Fixtures length_short_form_zero and item_zero_length.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: The BER-OID chain rule for ANY width, which is the '(or more)' ST 0601.14a SS 7.1 named and never defined.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: BER-OID tags are one or more bytes linked together in chain fashion. In BER-OID a zero in the Most Significant Bit (msb) position terminates the tag's chain. For example, when the msb is set to zero in the first byte, this forms a one-byte tag number ranging from 0x00 to 0x7F. When the msb of the first byte is set to one, the second successive byte becomes part of the BER-OID chain. In continued fashion, if the second byte's msb is set to one, the next byte becomes part of the chain. This pattern continues until the msb of a final byte in the chain is zero. Together the seven Least Signification Bits (lsb) of each byte in the chain form the tag number.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.second_statement_verbatim: Using BER-OID for the tags in all MISB local sets enables efficient tag encoding and unlimited future growth.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.this_was_a_residue_of_the_framing_round_: The framing round recorded 'BER-OID encodings three octets wide and beyond' as UNDERIVABLE and refused a third continuation octet, on the ground that extending Figure 67's pattern was 'arithmetic anybody can do, which is exactly what makes it the tempting reconstruction'. SS 6.3.1 states the general rule, so the extension is now a transcription. decode_ber_oid follows the chain and encode_ber_oid emits any non-negative integer.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.what_this_cost_in_the_codec: BER_OID_MAX_OCTETS is DELETED - a cap beside a codec that no longer honours it is a constant nothing reads. BER_OID_MAX is KEPT at 16383 and re-documented as a waypoint rather than a limit: it is what the delegating document could prove alone, and the exhaustive round-trip test still runs over it because the range fits in a test.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: klv_codec.decode_ber_oid and encode_ber_oid. Fixture tag_three_octet_lowest (818000 -> 16384) REPLACES the refusal fixture tag_third_continuation_octet (818100).

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: Non-minimal BER-OID tags are forbidden, on LIVE authority.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: To prevent BER-OID from including leading zeros, ASN.1 forbids the use of 0x80 in the first byte of a BER-OID value.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.this_is_a_PROMOTION_and_not_a_behaviour_: decode_ber_oid already refused a leading 0x80. The framing round recorded that refusal as 'UNDERIVABLE AS A NORM, DECIDED AS AN IMPLEMENTATION' because the only sentence requiring tag minimality in ST 0601.14a was ST 0601.8-06, marked (Deprecated), and it wrote: 'If ST 0107.3 turns out to require acceptance, this is the decision that changes.' IT DID NOT. ST 0107.3 forbids the octet by name, so the refusal is now transcribed rather than decided. The behaviour is identical and the provenance is not, and the caveat is recorded as discharged rather than deleted.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.one_honest_wrinkle: SS 6.3.1 attributes the prohibition to ASN.1 rather than asserting it as a numbered ST 0107.3 requirement - 'ASN.1 forbids'. So it is live prose in a held document reporting a rule from a document this repository does not hold. That is materially stronger than a deprecated requirement and materially weaker than a 'shall', and it is recorded at that strength rather than rounded up. Registered as KLV 13, which also notes that the reference it points at is X.680.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: klv_codec.decode_ber_oid's leading-0x80 refusal, whose message now quotes SS 6.3.1 and names ST 0601.8-06 as the deprecated predecessor. Fixture tag_non_minimal_two_octets.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: Bit and byte order are big-endian, KLV-wide and retroactively.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.locus: SS 6.1, 'Bit and Byte Order', PDF page 2. NOTE THE PREFIX: these two requirements are numbered ST 0107.2, not ST 0107.3.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: ST 0107.2-01 Bit order shall be big-endian or msb. / ST 0107.2-02 Byte order shall be big-endian or MSB.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.why_the_prefix_is_0107_2: MISB stamps a requirement with the edition that introduced it, and this edition's revision history says it 'Added requirements -03 through -13'. So -01 and -02 came from ST 0107.2 - registry document 4149, which 0107.3 supersedes - and keep their prefix. Citing them as ST 0107.3-01/-02 would cite strings this document does not contain.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.what_it_bears_on: decode_ber_length reads a long-form payload big-endian on ST 0107.2-02's authority, and it is the only octet-order rule in the chain: ST 0601.14a never states one. So the length codec's endianness is cited to a requirement whose number is not this edition's, which is exactly the sort of thing that gets miscited once and then propagates.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: int.from_bytes(payload, 'big') in klv_codec.decode_ber_length, with the requirement quoted at the line.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: A decoder must skip items it does not recognise, using the Length to find the next one.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: Applications which decode MISB KLV Local Sets shall skip unknown Local Set values so as to not impact the decoding of known Local Set items within the same Local Set instance.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.supporting_prose_verbatim: One advantage of KLV is the ability to skip or ignore items which may not be known by a consumer of the data. For example, suppose a new version of a Local Set introduces new tags which an existing decoder does not understand. Instead of crashing, the decoder simply ignores any item it does not understand - this makes a decoder 'future-proof'. In such cases, the Length specified by the Tag is used to skip the correct number of bytes to the next item.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.implemented_as: walk_local_set satisfies it STRUCTURALLY rather than with a skip list: it knows no tags at all, so every item is equally unknown to it and the caller decides what it recognises. The 141-row tag table is in this file and nothing in klv_codec consults it.

established_from_the_pinned_copy.rule: ST 0107.3 is a RESTRICTING profile of SMPTE ST 336, not a deferral to it.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.locus: SS 6.2, 'SMPTE KLV', PDF page 2, and ST 0107.3-03.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.verbatim: The MISB standards define requirements which incur limits on the full SMPTE 336, making the MISB standards a profile of the SMPTE standards.
established_from_the_pinned_copy.second_statement_verbatim: ST 0107.3-03 All Local Set KLV metadata shall be formatted in compliance with SMPTE ST 336 [1].
established_from_the_pinned_copy.why_this_matters_to_park_8: It is the answer to the round's question 'does 0107.3 add any constraint of its own on top of the delegation'. YES, and ST 0107.3-05's minimality is that constraint. Which is why the length codec is COMPLETE AND TOTAL with park 8 still open: the delegation widens what ST 336 would allow and ST 0107.3 narrows it, and the narrowed grammar is fully stated here.

underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.rule: 0x80 as a FIRST LENGTH OCTET - a long form declaring zero following octets.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.status: UNDERIVABLE FROM THE BYTES IN HAND. PARK 8. The one residue in the length grammar and the reason park 8 is not closed by this round.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.what_the_pinned_copy_does_say: NOTHING, and the silence is the finding. SS 6.3.2 defines the short form and the long form and never mentions a count of zero. In BER this is the INDEFINITE-LENGTH form, whose meaning is SMPTE ST 336's - and naming it as such is already at the edge of what this repository may assert, which is why the codec refuses rather than describing.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.the_delegating_sentence_verbatim: ST 0107.3-03 All Local Set KLV metadata shall be formatted in compliance with SMPTE ST 336 [1].
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.does_0107_3_add_a_constraint_on_top_of_t: NO, not for this octet. It adds ST 0107.3-05's minimality, which bears on every OTHER long form and cannot reach this one: 0x80 encodes no length at all, so 'fewest possible bytes' has nothing to compare. This is the one place in the grammar where the profile's restriction does not cover the delegation's surface.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.why_it_costs_nothing_today: A conforming encoder never emits it - ST 0107.3-05 makes every length's encoding unique and none of them is 0x80 - so the octet is unreachable from any stream this repository would write or any stream a conforming implementation would. It is reachable from a NON-conforming stream, which is exactly why the decoder must say something honest about it.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.implemented_as: klv_codec.decode_ber_length raises UnderivableFromPinnedCopy carrying park 8 and ST 0107.3-03. Fixture length_indefinite_first_octet, whose generator check asserts the exception TYPE so a later round cannot decide what 0x80 means without buying the document.

underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.rule: Any ceiling on the NUMBER of length octets.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.status: NOT STATED BY ST 0107.3. PARK 8, and recorded as an absence that was searched for rather than one that was assumed.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.what_the_pinned_copy_does_say: SS 6.3.2 states no maximum. The document's only maxima are elsewhere and govern a different quantity: SS 6.3.3 'items may have maximum lengths defined. When encoding a Value do not exceed the maximum limits', and ST 0107.3-07, 'Where a MISB standard defines a numeric maximum Length for a Local Set item's Value, the encoded Value shall not exceed the number of bytes defined by the maximum Length'. Both bound a VALUE's size, not a length field's width. The whole six pages were searched for 'maximum', 'limit', 'ceiling' and the numerals 127 and 128; the only occurrences are those two and SS 6.3.2's own 'values less than 128'.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.the_bound_the_codec_uses_is_STRUCTURAL_a: BER_LENGTH_OF_LENGTH_MAX = 127, because the first octet carries the long-form flag in bit 7 and the count in the remaining seven bits, so 127 is the largest count that octet can express. That is arithmetic on the shape SS 6.3.2's own examples fix, not a citation, and the constant's comment says so. Whether ST 336 imposes a LOWER ceiling is park 8's.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.implemented_as: encode_ber_length raises UnderivableFromPinnedCopy above the structural bound, carrying park 8 and the sentence that states no ceiling. Not KLVFramingError: a caller asking for a 128-octet length field is not handing over wrong bytes, they are asking a question this repository cannot answer.

underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.rule: Whether a DECODER must reject a non-minimal length.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.status: UNDERIVABLE AS A NORM, DECIDED AS AN IMPLEMENTATION - and the decision now rests on live authority, which is the difference from the framing round's version of this same entry.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.what_the_pinned_copy_does_say: ST 0107.3-05 is a 'shall' on the ENCODING: lengths 'shall be BER Short form or BER Long form encoded using the fewest possible bytes'. It does not say what a reader does when it meets a violation. SS 6.3.2's prose frames the two non-minimal forms as inefficient - 'BER becomes less efficient' - rather than as invalid, which pulls gently the other way.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.the_decision: klv_codec.decode_ber_length REFUSES both, as KLVFramingError - these bytes are wrong - because ST 0107.3-05 says they are wrong, in the live edition ST 0601.14a's live route points at. The second reason is the one the framing round gave for tags: accepting them would make several byte strings denote one length, and a round trip over an ambiguous encoding is a statement about the codec rather than about the wire.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.the_sentence_that_pulls_the_other_way_an: ST 0107.3-04 requires decoders to 'skip unknown Local Set values so as to not impact the decoding of known Local Set items', which is a be-permissive requirement. It is about unknown TAGS, not malformed lengths, and a decoder cannot honour it at all without first reading the length correctly - so a strict length reader is compatible with it. Recorded because the tension is real and an unstated tension reads as an unexamined one.
underivable_from_the_bytes_in_hand.what_is_not_claimed: That refusal is normatively required of a decoder. If a later ST 0107 or ST 336 requires acceptance, this is the decision that changes - and it is the same sentence the framing round wrote about the tag refusal, which is now discharged. This one is not.

value_encoding_requirements.what_this_is: The seven ST 0107.3 requirements that govern VALUES rather than framing, transcribed because ST 0107.3 SS 1 makes them retroactive - 'It applies retroactively to all documents approved by the Motion Imagery Standards Board (MISB)' - and because the round that writes a value decoder should not have to fetch this document again. NOTHING IN klv_codec IMPLEMENTS ANY OF THEM.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-06: Where a MISB standard defines a numeric required Length for a Local Set item's Value, the encoded Value shall match the number of bytes defined by the required Length.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-07: Where a MISB standard defines a numeric maximum Length for a Local Set item's Value, the encoded Value shall not exceed the number of bytes defined by the maximum Length.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-08: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of, or prefixed with, 'float,' the encoded Value shall use the IEEE 754-2008 [5] standard to encode the value.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-09: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of 'IMAPA' or 'IMAPB,' and the Local Set item allows variable length encoding, the encoded Value shall use the fewest number of bytes, while maintaining system precision.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-10: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of, or prefixed with, 'uint' or 'int,' and the Local Set item allows variable length encoding, the encoded value shall remove leading zero or leading sign extension bytes.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-11: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of 'ber' and the item allows variable length encoding, the encoded Value shall use the fewest number of bytes.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-12: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of 'utf8' and the Value is not the empty string, the encoded value shall have all leading and trailing, null (0x00), tab (0x09), line feed (0x0A), carriage return (0x0D), and space (0x20) characters removed, unless the item definition allows them.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-13: Where a MISB standard defines a Local Set item with a KLV format of 'utf8' and the Value is not the empty string, the encoded value shall have all characters in the hex ranges (inclusive) of 0x00 through 0x08, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0E through 0x1F, and character 0x7F removed, unless the item definition allows them.
value_encoding_requirements.the_empty_string_versus_the_unknown_stri: SS 6.3.3.2, and it is a distinction a value decoder will get wrong once: 'The emptystring uses a single null character (0x00) with no other characters to indicate the string is blank. The length of the emptystring within KLV is one (1), for the null character' and 'A string item with a length of zero (0) signifies an "Unknown" string.' So length 1 holding 0x00 is empty and length 0 is unknown, which are different CDM values and differ by one octet on the wire.
value_encoding_requirements.ST 0107.3-11_is_the_one_that_bears_on_th: It requires 'ber' TYPE VALUES to use the fewest bytes - a Value whose content is a BER length, which is a different thing from the Length field of an item. ST 0107.3-05 is the one that governs the Length field. The two say the same thing about different octets and it would be easy to cite the wrong one.
